body.statement: For every \(r>0\), the canonical modulus maximizer exists after irrelevant coordinates are set to zero; the resulting map \(r\mapsto h_r\) is Borel measurable. The modulus is finite, increasing, and concave, its right derivative is a Borel measurable supergradient, and \(\mathcal R_+\) is nonempty. For every \(r\in\mathcal R_+\), \(s_r>0\), \(b_r\) is the exact maximal absolute bias of \(\widehat\theta_r\), and each infimum-approaching sequence in the definition exists. Consequently every \(\widehat\theta_{r_{\mathrm{MSE},j}}\) and \(C_{\alpha,j}\) is a total measurable procedure even at radii where the modulus is nondifferentiable.
body.justification: A computable optimal-recovery rule must remain defined at exposed-face changes and must never divide by zero standard deviation.
body.gap: General modulus theory permits set-valued extremizers; this lemma supplies a total measurable selection for the finite staggered-DiD program used by the frontier.
body.consumer: Numerical convex programs can return reproducible weights and valid intervals at every admissible design point.
body.proof_tex:
Write \(\mathcal H=\mathcal M_{T,m}-\mathcal M_{T,m}=2\mathcal M_{T,m}\), where the equality follows from convexity and centrosymmetry.  The set \(\mathcal H\) is closed and convex.  For fixed \(r>0\), its intersection with \(\{h:\|Kh\|_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}^{-1}}\le r\}\) is effectively compact.  Indeed, the coordinates of the deviation component are bounded by \(2B\), all differences of calendar coordinates are bounded by \(2L\), and \(O\ne\varnothing\).  A bound on \(Kh\), together with the deviation bound at any row in \(O\), therefore bounds one calendar coordinate and hence all calendar coordinates.  Coordinates occurring in neither \(K\), \(\ell\), nor a centering equation may be set to zero.  The remaining set is a closed bounded subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.  The maximum defining \(\omega_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}}(r)\) is consequently attained.

Monotonicity is immediate from nesting of the norm balls.  If \(h_i\) is feasible at radius \(r_i\), then convexity of \(\mathcal H\) and the triangle inequality give
\[
 \|K\{\lambda h_1+(1-\lambda)h_2\}\|_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}^{-1}}
 \le \lambda r_1+(1-\lambda)r_2.
\]
Linearity of \(\ell\) and passage to suprema prove concavity.  Finiteness follows from compactness.

The graph of the argmax correspondence is closed: if \(r_i\to r\) and maximizing \(h_i\to h\), feasibility passes to the limit, while continuity and concavity imply \(\ell(h)=\omega_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}}(r)\).  On each compact radius interval, first minimize \(\|h\|_2\) over this graph and then successively minimize each coordinate over the surviving compact graph.  At each step the inverse image of \((-\infty,a)\) is a countable union of projections of compact sets obtained by restricting the radius to a compact interval and the objective to a rational margin.  It is Borel.  After finitely many coordinates the survivor is a singleton, proving that \(r\mapsto h_r\) is Borel.

Let \(p_r=\partial_+\omega_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}}(r)\).  The secant-slope inequalities for a finite concave function give
\[
 \omega(s)\le\omega(r)+p_r(s-r)\qquad(s>0),
\]
so \(p_r\) is a supergradient; it is decreasing and right-continuous and hence Borel.  Let \(d\) have calendar component identically one and deviation component zero.  Then \(ad\in\mathcal H\) for every \(a\in\mathbb R\), \(\ell(d)=1\), and \(Kd\ne0\).  Thus \(\omega(r)\) is unbounded as \(r\to\infty\).  Since it is increasing and concave, its right derivative cannot vanish at a finite radius.  A maximizer cannot have a slack norm constraint, because adding a sufficiently small positive multiple of \(d\) would preserve feasibility and strictly increase \(\ell\).  Hence \(p_r>0\) and \(\|Kh_r\|_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}^{-1}}=r\) for every \(r>0\), so \(\mathcal R_+=(0,\infty)\).

The supporting-hyperplane condition at \(h_r\) is
\[
 \ell(h)-\frac{p_r}{r}\langle Kh_r,Kh\rangle_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}^{-1}}
 \le\omega(r)-rp_r\qquad(h\in\mathcal H).
\]
Indeed, perturb \(h_r\) toward \(h\), apply the supergradient inequality, divide by the perturbation size, and use the directional derivative
\(r^{-1}\langle Kh_r,Kh-Kh_r\rangle_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}^{-1}}\) of the norm.  Applying the result to \(-h\) gives the corresponding absolute bound.

The exact Gaussian law now gives
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_x(\widehat\theta_r)
 =\left(\frac{p_r}{r}\right)^2\|Kh_r\|_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}^{-1}}^2
 =p_r^2=s_r^2.
\]
Since \(\mathcal H=2\mathcal M_{T,m}\), the support identity gives
\[
 \sup_{x\in\mathcal M_{T,m}}|\mathbb E_x\widehat\theta_r-\ell(x)|
 =\frac{\omega(r)-rp_r}{2}=b_r.
\]
Thus the exact maximal squared-error risk is \(b_r^2+s_r^2\).

Both infima in the definition are finite because \(r=1\) is admissible.  They are strictly positive: two distinct common-shift parameters \(\pm ad/2\), for fixed sufficiently small \(a>0\), induce equivalent, nonidentical Gaussian laws, so neither zero maximal squared-error risk nor a zero-length interval having coverage above one half at both points is possible.  Infimum-approaching radii with the stated multiplicative factors therefore exist.  Taking the least admissible radius in a fixed enumeration of rational intervals meeting each sublevel set makes the sequences deterministic.  All displayed procedures are Borel compositions of the selections already established.
